# Interlude — The Customer's Clock

**Read after Lab 4, before Lab 5** · no Factorio required · ~25 minutes

Every sink so far has been infinitely patient: it absorbed whatever
arrived, whenever it arrived, and throughput was the whole story. Lab 5
replaces it with a **customer** — demand that arrives on its own
schedule and stops being satisfiable 30 seconds later. This interlude
builds the measurement kit for that world, and it ends at the hardest
honesty problem in the course: what to report about a deadline you
never got to see.

## Demand is a flow with a deadline attached

The customer in Lab 5 demands 12 workpieces per minute, continuously.
Each unit of demand is created at a moment, joins a **backlog** if it
cannot be served immediately, and is filled strictly first-in-first-out.
Its **wait** is the time from creation to fulfillment, and the scenario
declares a maximum tolerable wait — the deadline.

Two rules keep the accounting honest:

- **FIFO, enforced.** The oldest unserved demand is always served first,
  so waits are well-defined and no analysis can quietly cherry-pick
  which customer got which item.
- **Surplus is not a bank.** Producing ahead of demand does not
  pre-credit customers who haven't asked yet; a delivery with no open
  demand behind it is recorded as surplus, full stop. (Real contracts
  work this way too: shipping early doesn't excuse shipping late next
  month.)

## The service metrics

**On-time item rate**: of all demanded items in the window, the fraction
fulfilled within their deadline. It is item-weighted — a cohort of ten
counts ten times a cohort of one — and it is a *service* number, not a
production number. That distinction has teeth: a line can run at full
throughput and still fail every deadline, if the timing is wrong.

**Wait percentiles** (Lab 5 uses p95): the wait that 95% of demanded
items beat. Averages flatter service systems — one customer served
instantly and one who waited a minute average to "30 s", which describes
neither. The tail is where customers live.

## Censoring: the deadline you didn't see

The run ends. Some demand near the end was created, its deadline still
in the future when observation stopped. What is it?

![Three fates for a unit of demand against an observation horizon. Only
the first two are verdicts; the third is an honest refusal to
issue one.](../images/interludes/censoring.svg){width=100%}

- Fulfilled within the deadline → **on time**. Final.
- Deadline observed passing unfulfilled → **late**. Final — note this
  needs no run-end: the verdict lands the instant the deadline passes,
  and later fulfillment cannot repair it.
- Deadline beyond the horizon → **unresolved**. Not on time, not late —
  *unknown*, and reported as exactly that.

The temptation is to fold unresolved units into whichever bucket
flatters the story ("not late yet" → on time). FISL's rules instead:
the on-time rate's window and horizon are declared so that reported
cohorts have observable deadlines (Lab 5's scenario adds a
`service_tail` phase for precisely this), and the wait percentile is
**strictly censored** — if any unit needed for the percentile is
unfulfilled, the metric refuses to print a number at all. You will see
`censored` in a real report in Lab 5, and it will be the most honest
cell in the table.

## Service, capacity, and the cost of a cap

The line's capacity is 15/min; the customer wants 12/min. That 25%
margin means 100% on-time service is *achievable* — and, remarkably,
achievable at wildly different WIP levels, which is the entire drama of
Lab 5: push and a well-tuned pull deliver identical service; only the
inventory differs.

But admission control has a cliff. Cap the line's intake *below* demand
— say at 10/min against 12 — and backlog grows at 2/min, forever.
Waits grow with the backlog; once the queue is longer than what the cap
can clear within the patience window, **every subsequent unit is late**.
The measured on-time rate then mostly reflects how early in the run the
queue outgrew the deadline — keep running and it decays toward zero.
One number to internalize: an over-tight cap doesn't degrade service
proportionally (10/12 ≈ 83%); it collapses it, because lateness
compounds through the queue.

## Claims to carry into Lab 5

1. The baseline (push) will serve 100% on time. So will a correctly
   tuned pull — with the *same* p95 wait — while carrying a fraction of
   the WIP. Service metrics alone cannot distinguish them; the ledger
   can.
2. The deliberately over-tight reference solution admits 10/min against
   12/min demand. Predict: on-time far below 83%, decaying with run
   length, and a p95 that prints `censored` rather than a number.
3. Little's Law works on the backlog too: the customer's average wait
   relates backlog and demand rate exactly as WIP relates to throughput
   and cycle time. One law, second appearance.

## Further reading

- Hopp & Spearman, *Factory Physics* (3rd ed.), ch. 10 "Push and Pull
  Production Systems" — the control side of what Lab 5 measures; ch. 3
  and 4 for where push (MRP) and pull (JIT) actually came from.
- Little & Graves, "Little's Law" (in *Building Intuition*, 2008) — §on
  applications includes exactly this waiting-line reading.
- The demand-cohort and censoring contract is FISL's ADR 0008.
